title: A contact sheet is the cheapest instrument check: same camera, same scene, and a flame in every tile
summary: A grid of frames sampled at fixed intervals across a run lets you see, before trusting any measurement, that the camera did not move, the flame stayed in frame and the scale reference is visible. It also documents runs whose scale anchor is in doubt.

media.alt: A contact sheet of eight greyscale video frames in three rows, labelled t = 303 s to t = 513 s in steps of 30 s, showing a bright flame above a thin vertical burner tube on a base plate, all with the same camera framing. The flame shape changes between tiles from a narrow tongue to a kinked, leaning or detached tip. The time labels at the top left of each tile are black on a dark background and hard to read.

source.caption: QC contact sheet — MVI_8036
source.note: Group explainer for the qc topic. The two sheets have the same layout and are read the same way; the caption of the second says its independent scale-anchor fit was flagged during review. The figure itself shows no scale numbers.
group: 28_MVI_8036-qc: QC contact sheet, MVI_8036 (8 frames, 303 to 513 s, representative figure)
29_MVI_8040-qc: QC contact sheet, MVI_8040 (9 frames, 234 to 474 s)

read_the_figure.question: Are the frames of this run consistent enough, in framing and content, to measure from?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes. Each tile is one video frame, greyscale, with the time since the start of the record in the upper left (the labels are black on dark, so they are nearly invisible). Tiles read left to right, top to bottom, spaced 30 s apart: t = 303, 333, ..., 513 s for MVI_8036; 234, 264, ..., 474 s for MVI_8040.
look_at: The burner tube and its base plate: the tube top and the base should sit at identical pixel positions in every tile. They do, in both sheets, so the camera did not move.
The flame position relative to the tube top: it always starts at the same point, so the burner exit is a stable reference for height.
The flame shapes: narrow tongue, leaning, kinked, bulged, detached tip. This shows the range the segmentation must handle, from a smooth flame to a broken one.
The background: dark curtain, a bench and a reflective strip on the bench. Bright reflections are the likely source of false detections.
The glow around the flame, and the saturated white core.
In MVI_8040, the same layout but the camera sees the scene slightly differently (tube and plate lower in the tile than in MVI_8036), which is why the scale must be fitted per run.
read_the_figure.proves: That the framing is stable within a run and that the flame stays in view, which are preconditions for converting pixels to millimetres with one scale per run. It does not prove that the scale value is right.
if_wrong: Tube or plate shifting between tiles: the camera or the burner moved, so a single pixel-to-mm scale is wrong for part of the record.
A flame touching the frame edge: height is truncated.
A reference feature that is ambiguous: the scale fit may lock onto the wrong feature (the caption says this happened for one run) and every millimetre value would be off by a constant factor.
Unreadable time labels: you cannot tie a tile to its time.
must_check: That the scale was derived from a feature of known size and that the feature is identified in the sheet.
That the sampling interval is stated and constant.
That tiles are drawn at the same size and crop.
That the run is compared with the inherited ensemble scale and the difference is reported.
as_drawn: MVI_8036: 8 tiles, 303 to 513 s, 30 s apart. MVI_8040: 9 tiles, 234 to 474 s, 30 s apart.
The tube tops sit at nearly the same tile position within each sheet (read by eye); the vertical position of the tube differs between the two sheets.
The caption states that MVI_8036's ruler-derived scale agrees with the ensemble's inherited scale to within 0.4 percent. That number is from the caption and cannot be checked on the figure.

terms.meaning: A grid of small frames sampled from a longer record, used to inspect it at a glance.
The factor that converts pixels to millimetres, found from a feature of known physical size in the image.
The reference feature used for the calibration, such as a ruler or the burner tube.
A scale carried over from a reference run to others, valid only if camera and zoom are unchanged.
Difference divided by the reference value, usually in percent.
Checks that data are fit for measurement before any result is drawn from them.
For a flat object at distance Z with focal length f the image size is f/Z times the object size, so the scale is the same across the object.

remember: A scale error is multiplicative: every length scales by it, every area by its square, every volume by its cube.
Scale = known size / size in pixels.
A stable tube position across tiles is evidence of a stable camera, not of a correct scale.
Always report the comparison between a run's own scale and an inherited one.
A QC figure that shows a problem honestly is more useful than one that hides it.
Tiny, dark labels are a design defect: they defeat the purpose of the sheet.

understand.title: What the sheet checks
understand.text: Three things: the camera did not move, the flame stays in frame, and the reference is visible. All three can be judged by eye in a minute, which is why it is the first QC step.

understand.title: Why the scale matters so much
understand.text: Everything in millimetres, such as height, width, area and volume, inherits the scale. A wrong anchor does not add noise, it rescales the whole run; that is why the sheet is kept as evidence rather than discarded.

understand.title: Why the two sheets differ in framing
understand.text: The tube and plate sit at different positions in the tiles of the two runs. Unless the camera setup is identical, an inherited scale cannot be assumed, so each run's scale is fitted or checked on its own.

steps.title: Scale from a known length
steps.note: A feature of known length in millimetres divided by its length in pixels. Length in millimetres is then pixels times s.

steps.title: Relative disagreement between two scales
steps.note: The measure behind 'within 0.4 percent'. Positive means the run's own scale is larger than the inherited one.

steps.title: How a scale error propagates
steps.note: A length goes as s, an area as s squared and a volume as s cubed, so a 0.4 percent scale error is about 0.8 percent in area and 1.2 percent in volume (first order).

steps.title: Uncertainty of the scale itself
steps.note: Standard propagation for a quotient of independent quantities, as in the GUM. A short reference, measured to a pixel or two, is the weak link.

steps.title: Wrong anchor: a constant factor
steps.note: If the fit picks a different feature whose pixel length is L-prime, every length is off by the ratio of the two pixel lengths. It is a pure factor, so ratios and dimensionless quantities such as CV are unaffected, while millimetre values are.

worked.title: What a 0.4 percent scale difference does
worked.problem: A flame height is reported as 100 mm using the inherited scale, and the run's own scale is 0.4 percent smaller. What are the height, the area (taken as 1000 mm squared) and the volume (10000 mm cubed) with the run's own scale?
worked.answer: 99.6 mm, about 992 mm squared and about 9880 mm cubed: decreases of 0.4, 0.8 and 1.2 percent. The three starting values are teaching numbers, not from the figure.

analyze.q: In the sheet for MVI_8040 the tube sits lower in the tile than in MVI_8036. What does that imply for using one scale for both runs, and what would you measure to settle it?
Some tiles show a bright detached wisp above the flame. How would that affect a height measure, and where in the processing would you handle it?
Which of height, width, CV and volume change if the scale is off by a constant factor?

evaluate.q: The sheet shows a run with a doubtful scale anchor. Is it right to publish it? What should accompany it?
evaluate.hint: Say what was found and what was done about it.

evaluate.q: Is a contact sheet sufficient QC for a campaign?
evaluate.hint: It checks framing, not calibration accuracy or exposure.

create: Redesign the sheet: legible time labels, the scale reference marked, a ruler in the tile, and the fitted scale printed under each sheet.
Define an automatic check that flags tube movement between tiles and say what threshold you would use.

checks.q: What does a stable tube position across tiles show?
checks.answer: That the camera and burner did not move, so a single scale applies to the whole run. It does not show the scale value is right.

checks.q: A scale is 0.5 percent too large. By what percent is a volume too large?
If the scale fit locked onto the wrong feature, what happens to a coefficient of variation?
checks.answer: Nothing: CV is a ratio of two lengths and the constant factor cancels. Millimetre values do change.

checks.q: Why keep a sheet for a run with a flagged scale?
checks.answer: It is the evidence for the finding. Hiding it would remove the reason the run is treated differently.

checks.q: What would you add so the sheet checks the scale as well as the framing?
checks.answer: A ruler or a marked feature of known size in the first tile, with its pixel length and the fitted scale printed on the sheet.
